Title: Why draw when you can Withdraw?

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
On 11-JUL-2003, Curevei (cur...@aol.commetal) wrote:
>>>No. You cannot force a player to trust another player to honor a deal.
>>
>>LSJ has really hit the nail on the head with this part.
>>
>>There's really an important trust issue with attempts to withdrawals. For the
>>judges who simply allow a table withdrawal since everyone "agrees" to a
>>withdrawal, he might be foiling the plans of one of the players who plans to
>>do
>>a 180 at the last minute.
>>
>>Similarly, a player who has the advantage in permanents might very well want
>>to
>>see the combat monster or intercept wall deck run out of cards this way.
>
> I don't find the idea of someone breaking a mutual withdrawal plan realistic.
> Since it takes so little time to accomplish, might as well wait til the last
> few minutes. Since it takes a bunch of time to oust people you were thinking
> of agreeing to withdraw with, you won't have time to oust once you enact your
> withdrawal plan. If there's a big disparity in permanents, the plan is
> unlikely to occur or likely to occur only so late as to make it impossible to
> oust anyone. It's easy enough to see someone trying to back out of an
> agreement, which leaves the game in basically the same situation if everyone
> stops turbowithdrawing. If you can oust someone whether with the "perfect
> hand" or not, there was never any basis for a withdrawal agreement in the first
> place.
>
> I think more credit should be given to players. The agree to a draw rule
> serves no purpose. There's no benefit to playing out a mutual withdrawal.

FYI, it came up at the final North American qualifier at Gen*Con this year.

The players agreed to withdraw and proceeded taking their "default" turns
of "untap, discard, I'm done". Until one player took his real turn and ousted
his prey. Then the players that remained reinstated the deal and finished
out with the default turns until all but one had withdrawn.

I'm glad I gave more credit to the players than to force them to honor the
deal or not make it at all. (Although the player who was ousted was upset
at my making them play it out.)

>
>I'm glad I gave more credit to the players than to force them to honor the
>deal or not make it at all. (Although the player who was ousted was upset
>at my making them play it out.)

Wouldn't that be giving them a lack of credit as a mutual withdrawal deal makes
no sense when one player could oust a prey by taking one turn?

I guess I've been giving people too much credit, figuring that they would pay
close attention to any deal that would result in the game ending.

To stop the "mutual withdrawal bluff" only requires players to come up with
such measures as everyone setting their hands face down, discarding from one
"side" and replacing to the other without ever looking at cards drawn or, even
more tedious, such as another player chooses which card you discard - third
from my left, one of the cards you didn't just draw, or whatever - and, if the
player doesn't agree, then the deal is broken.

At the great cost of making a fair number of games tedious by forcing people to
play out a stalemated situation, you get a trivial benefit that a player(s)
making a bad deal gets punished by throwing away a game that could have been
stalled out instead.

Messages.Author: Janne Hägglund
Messages.Body:
cur...@aol.commetal (Curevei) writes:

> Once you establish that an agreement to mutually withdraw resolves
> immediately, you can save quite a bit of time.

And eliminate any change of bluffing, backstabbing, mind games, broken
deals, Evil Deeds, paranoia,...

One thing I love about VTES is that you can never be sure of anything.
You don't know what your opponent has in his hand, you don't know how he
will respond to your move, *you don't know if he will keep his deal or not.*

I enjoy games that end with "he did WHAT???" much, much more than games
that end with anticlimactic "and then everyone did as we together planned
to do."

I don't want to play a game where I *know* what is going to happen.
I want to play a game where I always have to be careful, always on my toes.

Waiting to the last minute was pointed out as a solution if you didn't trust
people. If you don't have to trust people, then you can save a lot of time.

Might be a case of losing the forest for the trees. The original post fit the
title well - why draw for half a VP when withdrawing is a whole VP? Well, the
only reason may be because agreeing to draw just happens (as I recall, I really
don't care since it's nigh unto useless as a mechanic) but, important to later
posts, withdrawing requires going through some rigmarole ... if you play it
out. My take was that it isn't worth playing out because the basis for
agreeing to withdraw is a stalemated situation with not a sufficient amount of
time for people to think they will oust anyone.

When this occurs can vary tremendously, of course. In the case of little time
being left, the savings of not going through the motions is not going through
the motions. Besides being less tedious, when you know you can withdraw with
30 seconds left or whatever, you can afford to play longer without such an
agreement. Isn't this what people want people to do - play games out as much
as possible?

In the case that a game is horribly stalemated with a significant amount of
time left, you can produce a faster tournament and, yet again, not have to put
effort into doing something that shouldn't serve any purpose.

>(with

>The ousted player may have figured that a 90% chance at a full VP
>was better than a 99.9% chance at a half VP finish (or whatever the
>probabilities were).

The problem with this example isn't the ousted player agreeing to the deal.
It's that the player able to oust someone in one turn would agree to such a
deal. If someone can take a turn and get a VP, I'm not seeing any basis for a
mutual withdrawal deal.

I want to expand on something in the above paragraph that I don't see people
getting. The ousted player should have been ousted anyway. So, he/she lost
nothing by the agreement. A badly conceived mutual withdrawal deal only hurts
people who could do better.

People are trying to argue that there's a treachery basis, that you can mess
someone up somehow by making them think you won't come after them. I've just
been giving examples in a number of these posts of how players can counter that
such that this should never come about in a real situation. The treachery
counters, which can be tedious themselves, wouldn't be necessary if the
agreement ended the game immediately.
